{{Short description|State of matter with insulating bulk but conductive boundary}}
{{science review|date=February 2024}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
[[File:Topological insulator informal phase diagram-en.svg|thumb|An (informal) phase diagram with topological insulators, trivial insulators, and conductors. There is no path from the topological insulators to the trivial insulators that does not cross the conducting phase. The diagram depicts a <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>topological invariant, since there are two "islands" of insulators.]]
[[File:Topological insulator band structure.svg|thumb|An idealized [[band structure]] for a 3D time-reversal symmetric topological insulator. The [[Fermi level]] falls within the bulk band gap which is traversed by topologically-protected spin-textured Dirac surface states.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Moore|first=Joel E.|date=2010|title=The birth of topological insulators|journal=Nature|language=En|volume=464|issue=7286|pages=194–198|doi=10.1038/nature08916|issn=0028-0836|pmid=20220837|bibcode=2010Natur.464..194M|s2cid=1911343}}</ref><ref name="HM">{{Cite journal|last1=Hasan|first1=M.Z. |last2=Moore|first2=J.E.  |date=2011|title=Three-Dimensional Topological Insulators|journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics|language=En|volume=2|pages=55–78|doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-062910-140432|bibcode=2011ARCMP...2...55H|arxiv=1011.5462|s2cid=11516573 }}</ref>]]
A '''topological insulator''' is a material whose interior behaves as an [[electrical insulator]] while its surface behaves as an [[Electrical conductivity|electrical conductor]],<ref name="KM">{{Cite journal|last = Kane | first = C. L.  |author2=Mele, E. J.   | year = 2005 | title = Z<sub>2</sub> Topological Order and the Quantum Spin Hall Effect | journal = [[Physical Review Letters]] | volume = 95 | issue = 14 | article-number = 146802 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.146802 | pmid = 16241681  | bibcode=2005PhRvL..95n6802K|arxiv = cond-mat/0506581 | s2cid = 1775498 }}</ref> meaning that electrons can only move along the surface of the material.

A topological insulator is an insulator for the same reason a "[[Triviality (mathematics)|trivial]]" (ordinary) insulator is: there exists an [[Band gap|energy gap]] between the [[valence and conduction bands]] of the material. But in a topological insulator, these bands are, in an informal sense, "twisted", relative to a trivial insulator.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Zhiyong |last2=Cheng |first2=Yingchun |last3=Schwingenschlögl |first3=Udo |date=2012-06-01 |title=Band inversion mechanism in topological insulators: A guideline for materials design |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.85.235401 |journal=Physical Review B |language=en |volume=85 |issue=23 |article-number=235401 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.85.235401 |bibcode=2012PhRvB..85w5401Z |hdl=10754/315777 |issn=1098-0121|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The topological insulator cannot be [[Continuous function|continuously]] transformed into a trivial one without untwisting the bands, which closes the band gap and creates a conducting state. Thus, due to the continuity of the underlying field, the [[Surface state|border]] of a topological insulator with a trivial insulator (including [[vacuum]], which is topologically trivial) is forced to support conducting [[edge states]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Qi |first1=Xiao-Liang |last2=Zhang |first2=Shou-Cheng |date=2011-10-14 |title=Topological insulators and superconductors |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.83.1057 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |language=en |volume=83 |issue=4 |pages=1057–1110 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.83.1057 |arxiv=1008.2026 |bibcode=2011RvMP...83.1057Q |s2cid=118373714 |issn=0034-6861}}</ref>

Since this results from a global property of the topological insulator's [[band structure]], local (symmetry-preserving) perturbations cannot damage this surface state.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last1=Hasan |first1=M. Z. |last2=Kane |first2=C. L. |date=2010-11-08 |title=Colloquium: Topological insulators |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.82.3045 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=3045–3067 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.82.3045|bibcode=2010RvMP...82.3045H |s2cid=16066223 |arxiv=1002.3895 }}</ref> This is unique to topological insulators: while ordinary insulators can also support conductive surface states, only the surface states of topological insulators have this robustness property.

This leads to a more formal definition of a topological insulator: an insulator which cannot be [[Adiabatic theorem|adiabatically]] transformed into an ordinary insulator without passing through an intermediate conducting state.<ref name=":10" /> In other words, topological insulators and trivial insulators are separate regions in the [[phase diagram]], connected only by conducting phases. In this way, topological insulators provide an example of a [[state of matter]] not described by the [[Landau theory|Landau symmetry-breaking theory]] that defines ordinary states of matter.<ref name=":11" />

The properties of topological insulators and their surface states are highly dependent on both the dimension of the material and its underlying [[Symmetry in quantum mechanics|symmetries]], and can be classified using the so-called [[Periodic table of topological invariants|periodic table of topological insulators]]. Some combinations of dimension and symmetries forbid topological insulators completely.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Kitaev |first=Alexei |author-link1=Alexei Kitaev |date=2009-05-14 |title=Periodic table for topological insulators and superconductors |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/abs/10.1063/1.3149495 |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1134 |issue=1 |pages=22–30 |doi=10.1063/1.3149495 |arxiv=0901.2686 |bibcode=2009AIPC.1134...22K |s2cid=14320124 |issn=0094-243X}}</ref> All topological insulators have at least [[U(1)|U(1) symmetry]] from [[particle number]] conservation, and often have [[time-reversal symmetry]] from the absence of a magnetic field. In this way, topological insulators are an example of [[symmetry-protected topological order]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Senthil |first=T. |date=2015-03-01 |title=Symmetry-Protected Topological Phases of Quantum Matter |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031214-014740 |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |language=en |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=299–324 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031214-014740 |arxiv=1405.4015 |bibcode=2015ARCMP...6..299S |s2cid=12669555 |issn=1947-5454}}</ref> So-called "topological invariants", taking values in <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>&nbsp;or <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, allow classification of insulators as trivial or topological, and can be computed by various methods.<ref name=":12" />

The surface states of topological insulators can have exotic properties. For example, in time-reversal symmetric 3D topological insulators, surface states have their [[Spin quantum number|spin]] locked at a right-angle to their momentum (spin-momentum locking). At a given energy the only other available electronic states have different spin, so [[Umklapp scattering|"U"-turn scattering]] is strongly suppressed and conduction on the surface is highly metallic.

Despite their origin in quantum mechanical systems, analogues of topological insulators can also be found in classical media. There exist [[Photonic topological insulator|photonic]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Khanikaev |first1=Alexander B. |last2=Hossein Mousavi |first2=S. |last3=Tse |first3=Wang-Kong |last4=Kargarian |first4=Mehdi |last5=MacDonald |first5=Allan H. |last6=Shvets |first6=Gennady |date=March 2013 |title=Photonic topological insulators |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nmat3520 |journal=Nature Materials |language=en |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=233–239 |doi=10.1038/nmat3520 |pmid=23241532 |arxiv=1204.5700 |bibcode=2013NatMa..12..233K |s2cid=39748656 |issn=1476-4660}}</ref> [[Magnetic topological insulators|magnetic]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tokura |first1=Yoshinori |last2=Yasuda |first2=Kenji |last3=Tsukazaki |first3=Atsushi |date=February 2019 |title=Magnetic topological insulators |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s42254-018-0011-5 |journal=Nature Reviews Physics |language=en |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=126–143 |doi=10.1038/s42254-018-0011-5 |bibcode=2019NatRP...1..126T |s2cid=53694955 |issn=2522-5820|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[Acoustics|acoustic]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=He |first1=Cheng |last2=Ni |first2=Xu |last3=Ge |first3=Hao |last4=Sun |first4=Xiao-Chen |last5=Chen |first5=Yan-Bin |last6=Lu |first6=Ming-Hui |last7=Liu |first7=Xiao-Ping |last8=Chen |first8=Yan-Feng |date=December 2016 |title=Acoustic topological insulator and robust one-way sound transport |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nphys3867 |journal=Nature Physics |language=en |volume=12 |issue=12 |pages=1124–1129 |doi=10.1038/nphys3867 |arxiv=1512.03273 |bibcode=2016NatPh..12.1124H |s2cid=119255437 |issn=1745-2473}}</ref> topological insulators, among others.

== Prediction ==
The first models of 3D topological insulators were proposed by B. A. Volkov and O. A. Pankratov in 1985,<ref name=Volkov85>{{Cite journal|last1=Volkov|first1=B. A.|last2=Pankratov|first2=O. A.|date=1985-08-25|title=Two-dimensional massless electrons in an inverted contact |url=http://jetpletters.ru/ps/1420/article_21570.shtml|journal=JETP Letters|language=en|volume=42|issue=4|pages=178–181}}</ref> 
and subsequently by Pankratov, S. V. Pakhomov, and Volkov in 1987.<ref name=Pankratov87>{{Cite journal|last1=Pankratov|first1=O. A.|last2=Pakhomov|first2=S. V.|last3=Volkov|first3=B. A.|date=1987-01-01|title=Supersymmetry in heterojunctions: Band-inverting contact on the basis of Pb1-xSnxTe and Hg1-xCdxTe|journal=Solid State Communications|language=en|volume=61|issue=2|pages=93–96|doi=10.1016/0038-1098(87)90934-3|bibcode=1987SSCom..61...93P|issn=0038-1098}}</ref> Gapless 2D Dirac states were shown to exist at the band inversion contact in [[PbTe]]/[[SnTe]]<ref name=Volkov85/> and [[HgTe]]/[[CdTe]]<ref name=Pankratov87/> heterostructures. 
Existence of interface Dirac states in HgTe/CdTe was experimentally verified by [[Laurens W. Molenkamp]]'s group in 2D topological insulators in 2007.<ref name="König07">{{Cite journal|last1=König|first1=Markus|last2=Wiedmann|first2=Steffen|last3=Brüne|first3=Christoph|last4=Roth|first4=Andreas|last5=Buhmann|first5=Hartmut|last6=Molenkamp|first6=Laurens W.|last7=Qi|first7=Xiao-Liang|last8=Zhang|first8=Shou-Cheng|date=2007-11-02|title=Quantum Spin Hall Insulator State in HgTe Quantum Wells|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1148047|journal=Science|language=en|volume=318|issue=5851|pages=766–770|doi=10.1126/science.1148047|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17885096|arxiv=0710.0582|bibcode=2007Sci...318..766K|s2cid=8836690}}</ref>

Later sets of theoretical models for the 2D topological insulator (also known as the quantum spin Hall insulators) were proposed by [[Charles L. Kane]] and [[Eugene J. Mele]] in 2005,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kane|first1=C. L.|last2=Mele|first2=E. J.|date=2005-11-23|title=Quantum Spin Hall Effect in Graphene|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.226801|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=95|issue=22|article-number=226801|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.226801|pmid=16384250|arxiv=cond-mat/0411737|bibcode=2005PhRvL..95v6801K|s2cid=6080059}}</ref> and also by [[B. Andrei Bernevig]] and [[Shoucheng Zhang]] in 2006.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bernevig|first1=B. Andrei|last2=Zhang|first2=Shou-Cheng|date=2006-03-14|title=Quantum Spin Hall Effect|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.106802|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=96|issue=10|article-number=106802|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.106802|pmid=16605772|arxiv=cond-mat/0504147|bibcode=2006PhRvL..96j6802B|s2cid=2618285}}</ref> The <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topological invariant was constructed and the importance of the time reversal symmetry was clarified in the work by Kane and Mele.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kane|first1=C. L.|last2=Mele|first2=E. J.|date=2005-09-28|title=${Z}_{2}$ Topological Order and the Quantum Spin Hall Effect|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.146802|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=95|issue=14|article-number=146802|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.146802|pmid=16241681|arxiv=cond-mat/0506581|bibcode=2005PhRvL..95n6802K |s2cid=1775498}}</ref> Subsequently, Bernevig, Taylor L. Hughes and Zhang made a theoretical prediction that 2D topological insulator with one-dimensional (1D) helical edge states would be realized in quantum wells (very thin layers) of mercury telluride sandwiched between cadmium telluride.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bernevig|first1=B. Andrei|last2=Hughes|first2=Taylor L.|last3=Zhang|first3=Shou-Cheng|date=2006-12-15|title=Quantum Spin Hall Effect and Topological Phase Transition in HgTe Quantum Wells|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1133734|journal=Science|language=en|volume=314|issue=5806|pages=1757–1761|doi=10.1126/science.1133734|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17170299|arxiv=cond-mat/0611399|bibcode=2006Sci...314.1757B|s2cid=7295726}}</ref> The transport due to 1D helical edge states was indeed observed in the experiments by Molenkamp's group in 2007.<ref name="König07"/>

Although the topological classification and the importance of time-reversal symmetry were pointed in the 2000s, all the necessary ingredients and physics of topological insulators were already understood in the works from the 1980s.

In 2007, it was predicted that 3D topological insulators might be found in binary compounds involving [[bismuth]],<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevB.79.195322 | volume = 79 | article-number = 195322 | last = Roy | first = Rahul  | title = Three dimensional topological invariants for time reversal invariant Hamiltonians and the three dimensional quantum spin Hall effect| journal = Physical Review B | date = 2009-05-21 |arxiv = cond-mat/0607531 | s2cid = 119407081 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.106803 | volume = 98 | issue =  10| article-number = 106803 | author1= Liang Fu|author2= C. L. Kane|author3=E. J. Mele  | title = Topological insulators in three dimensions| journal = Physical Review Letters  | date = 2007-03-07 | pmid = 17358555 |arxiv = cond-mat/0607699| bibcode = 2007PhRvL..98j6803F | s2cid = 6037351 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevB.76.045302 | volume = 76 | issue = 4 | article-number = 045302 | last = Fu | first = Liang |author2=C. L. Kane  | title = Topological insulators with inversion symmetry | journal = Physical Review B | date = 2007-07-02 |arxiv = cond-mat/0611341 |bibcode = 2007PhRvB..76d5302F | s2cid = 15011491 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1088/1367-2630/9/9/356 | issn = 1367-2630 | volume = 9 | issue = 9 | page = 356 | last = Shuichi Murakami | title = Phase transition between the quantum spin Hall and insulator phases in 3D: emergence of a topological gapless phase | journal = New Journal of Physics | year = 2007 |arxiv = 0710.0930 |bibcode = 2007NJPh....9..356M | s2cid = 13999448 }}</ref> and in particular "strong topological insulators" exist that cannot be reduced to multiple copies of the [[Quantum spin Hall effect|quantum spin Hall state]].<ref>{{Cite journal| last = Kane | first = C. L. |author2=Moore, J. E.  | year = 2011 | title = Topological Insulators | journal = [[Physics World]] | volume =  24 | issue =   2| pages = 32–36 | doi =  10.1088/2058-7058/24/02/36| url = http://physics.gmu.edu/~pnikolic/articles/Topological%20insulators%20(Physics%20World,%20February%202011).pdf | bibcode = 2011PhyW...24b..32K }}</ref>

==Properties and applications==
Spin-momentum locking<ref name="Hsieh09">{{Cite journal |last1=Hsieh |first1=D. |last2=Xia |first2=Y. |last3=Qian |first3=D. |last4=Wray |first4=L. |display-authors=etal |date=2009 |title=A tunable topological insulator in the spin helical Dirac transport regime |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08234 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=460 |issue=7259 |pages=1101–5 |arxiv=1001.1590 |bibcode=2009Natur.460.1101H |doi=10.1038/nature08234 |issn=1476-4687 |pmid=19620959 |s2cid=4369601}}</ref> in the topological insulator allows symmetry-protected surface states to host [[Majorana particle]]s if superconductivity is induced on the surface of 3D topological insulators via proximity effects.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.096407| last = Fu | first = L. |author2=C. L. Kane  | title = Superconducting Proximity Effect and Majorana Fermions at the Surface of a Topological Insulator| journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 100 | issue =  9| article-number = 096407| year = 2008 | pmid = 18352737| bibcode=2008PhRvL.100i6407F|arxiv = 0707.1692 | s2cid = 7618062 | url = https://repository.upenn.edu/physics_papers/99 }}</ref> (Note that Majorana zero-mode can also appear without topological insulators.<ref name="Potter">{{cite journal | last1=Potter | first1=Andrew C. | last2=Lee | first2=Patrick A. | title=Topological superconductivity and Majorana fermions in metallic surface states | journal=Physical Review B | volume=85 | issue=9 | article-number=094516 | date=23 March 2012 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.85.094516 | arxiv=1201.2176 | bibcode=2012PhRvB..85i4516P | s2cid=59462024 }}</ref>) The non-trivialness of topological insulators is encoded in the existence of a gas of [[helical Dirac fermion]]s. Dirac particles which behave like massless relativistic fermions have been observed in 3D topological insulators. Note that the gapless surface states of topological insulators differ from those in the [[quantum Hall effect]]: the gapless surface states of topological insulators are symmetry-protected (i.e., not topological), while the gapless surface states in quantum Hall effect are topological (i.e., robust against any local perturbations that can break all the symmetries). The <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topological invariants cannot be measured using traditional transport methods, such as spin Hall conductance, and the transport is not quantized by the <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> invariants. An experimental method to measure <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topological invariants was demonstrated which provide a measure of the <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topological order.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1126/science.1167733 | last = Hsieh | first = D. |author2=D. Hsieh |author3=Y. Xia |author4=L. Wray |author5=D. Qian |author6=A. Pal |author7=J. H. Dil |author8=F. Meier |author9=J. Osterwalder |author10=C. L. Kane |author11=G. Bihlmayer |author12=Y. S. Hor |author13=R. J. Cava |author14=M. Z. Hasan | title = Observation of Unconventional Quantum Spin Textures in Topological Insulators| journal = Science | volume = 323 | issue = 5916 | pages = 919–922 | year = 2009 | pmid = 19213915|bibcode = 2009Sci...323..919H | arxiv = 0902.2617 | s2cid = 118353248 }}</ref>  (Note that the term [[Spin liquid|<math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topological order]] has also been used to describe the [[topological order]] with emergent <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> [[gauge theory]] discovered in 1991.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Read | first1 = N. | last2 = Sachdev | first2 = Subir | year = 1991 | title = Large-N expansion for frustrated quantum antiferromagnets | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 66 | issue = 13| pages = 1773–6 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.66.1773|bibcode = 1991PhRvL..66.1773R | pmid=10043303}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Wen | first1 = Xiao-Gang | year = 1991 | title = Mean Field Theory of Spin Liquid States with Finite Energy Gaps | journal = Phys. Rev. B | volume = 44 | issue = 6| pages = 2664–2672 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.44.2664| pmid = 9999836 |bibcode = 1991PhRvB..44.2664W }}</ref>) More generally (in what is known as the ''ten-fold way'') for each spatial dimensionality, each of the ten Altland—Zirnbauer symmetry classes of [[Random matrix|random Hamiltonians]] labelled by the type of discrete symmetry (time-reversal symmetry, particle-hole symmetry, and chiral symmetry) has a corresponding group of topological invariants (either <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> or trivial) as described by the [[periodic table of topological invariants]].<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.035005 | last = Chiu| first = C. |author2=J. Teo|author3=A. Schnyder |author4=S. Ryu  | title = Classification of topological quantum matter with symmetries| journal = Rev. Mod. Phys.| volume = 88 | issue = 35005 | article-number = 035005| year = 2016 | arxiv = 1505.03535| bibcode = 2016RvMP...88c5005C| s2cid = 119294876}}</ref>

The most promising applications of topological insulators are spintronic devices and dissipationless [[transistor]]s for [[quantum computer]]s based on the [[quantum spin Hall effect|quantum Hall effect]]<ref name="König07" /> and [[quantum anomalous Hall effect]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=Cui-Zu|last2=Zhang|first2=Jinsong|last3=Feng|first3=Xiao|last4=Shen|first4=Jie|last5=Zhang|first5=Zuocheng|last6=Guo|first6=Minghua|last7=Li|first7=Kang|last8=Ou|first8=Yunbo|last9=Wei|first9=Pang|date=2013-04-12|title=Experimental Observation of the Quantum Anomalous Hall Effect in a Magnetic Topological Insulator|journal=Science|language=en|volume=340|issue=6129|pages=167–170|doi=10.1126/science.1234414|issn=0036-8075|pmid=23493424|arxiv=1605.08829|bibcode=2013Sci...340..167C|s2cid=29455044}}</ref> In addition, topological insulator materials have also found practical applications in advanced [[Magnetoelectronics|magnetoelectronic]] and [[optoelectronic]] devices.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yue|first1=Zengji|last2=Cai|first2=Boyuan|last3=Wang|first3=Lan|last4=Wang|first4=Xiaolin|last5=Gu|first5=Min|date=2016-03-01|title=Intrinsically core-shell plasmonic dielectric nanostructures with ultrahigh refractive index|journal=Science Advances|language=en|volume=2|issue=3|article-number=e1501536|doi=10.1126/sciadv.1501536|issn=2375-2548|pmc=4820380|pmid=27051869|bibcode=2016SciA....2E1536Y}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yue|first1=Zengji|last2=Xue|first2=Gaolei|last3=Liu|first3=Juan|last4=Wang|first4=Yongtian|last5=Gu|first5=Min|date=2017-05-18|title=Nanometric holograms based on a topological insulator material|journal=Nature Communications|language=en|volume=8|article-number=ncomms15354|doi=10.1038/ncomms15354|doi-access=free|pmc=5454374|pmid=28516906|bibcode=2017NatCo...815354Y}}</ref>

=== Thermoelectrics ===
Some of the most well-known topological insulators are also [[thermoelectric materials]], such as Bi<sub>2</sub>Te<sub>3</sub> and its alloys with Bi<sub>2</sub>Se<sub>3</sub> (n-type thermoelectrics) and Sb<sub>2</sub>Te<sub>3</sub> (p-type thermoelectrics).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Witting |first1=Ian T. |last2=Chasapis |first2=Thomas C. |last3=Ricci |first3=Francesco |last4=Peters |first4=Matthew |last5=Heinz |first5=Nicholas A. |last6=Hautier |first6=Geoffroy |last7=Snyder |first7=G. Jeffrey |date=June 2019 |title=The Thermoelectric Properties of Bismuth Telluride |journal=Advanced Electronic Materials |language=en |volume=5 |issue=6 |doi=10.1002/aelm.201800904 |doi-access=free |issn=2199-160X|hdl=2078.1/215159 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> High thermoelectric power conversion efficiency is realized in materials with low thermal conductivity, high electrical conductivity, and high [[Seebeck coefficient]] (i.e., the incremental change in voltage due to an incremental change in temperature). Topological insulators are often composed of heavy atoms, which tends to lower thermal conductivity and are therefore beneficial for thermoelectrics. A recent study also showed that good electrical characteristics (i.e., high electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient) can arise in topological insulators due to warping of the bulk band structure, which is driven by band inversion.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Toriyama |first1=Michael |title=Are Topological Insulators Promising Thermoelectrics? |date=2023-11-06 |url=https://chemrxiv.org/engage/chemrxiv/article-details/6545ba97c573f893f1c4221d |access-date=2024-01-07 |language=en |doi=10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-3nvl3 |last2=Snyder |first2=G. Jeffrey}}</ref> Often, the electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient are conflicting properties of thermoelectrics and difficult to optimize simultaneously. Band warping, induced by band inversion in a topological insulator, can mediate the two properties by reducing the effective mass of electrons/holes and increasing the valley degeneracy (i.e., the number of electronic bands that are contributing to charge transport). As a result, topological insulators are generally interesting candidates for thermoelectric applications.

== Theoretical background ==

=== Topology of the Brillouin zone ===
[[File:Ebene_zu_Torus_verkleben_01.png|thumb|319x319px|When one glues the opposite edges of the two dimensional plane, one obtains a torus. This is the appropriate construction to describe the two-dimensional Brillouin zone, where opposite edges differ by a reciprocal lattice vector.]]
A periodic system is, by definition, invariant under some translations, allowing us to label the [[Quantum state|eigenstates]] of a periodic [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] by the eigenvalues of the [[Translation operator (quantum mechanics)|translation operators]] that leave the system unchanged. The eigenvalues of the translation operator are called [[Crystal momentum|crystal momenta]] (or quasimomenta) and are usually written as <math>\mathbf{k}=(k_1,k_2,...,k_d)</math> (where d is the number of dimensions of the system). Those [[quantum number]]s play a role analogous to the [[Wave vector|wavevector]] of a [[Free particle (quantum physics)|free particle]]. The periodicity of the crystal induces a periodicity in k-space: <math>\mathbf{k}</math> and <math>\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}</math>, where <math>\mathbf{G}</math> is a [[Reciprocal lattice|reciprocal wavevector]], describe the same state (or sets of states). The set of all quasimomenta that are not equivalent up to a reciprocal wavevector is called the [[Brillouin zone]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kittel |first=Charles |title=Introduction to Solid State Physics |date=1953 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc |isbn=0-471-41526-X |edition=8th |publication-date=}}</ref>  As a consequence of the periodicity of the Brillouin zone, its opposite edges or faces should be identified with each other, therefore the Brillouin zone describes a d-dimensional [[torus]], <math>T^d</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Girvin |first=Steven M. |title=Modern Condensed Matter Physics |last2=Yang |first2=Kun |date=2019 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-13739-4 |doi=10.1017/9781316480649}}</ref>

=== Two-band Hamiltonians ===
The topological insulators that are easiest to describe are periodic crystalline insulators with two degrees of freedom (e.g. two orbitals) per [[unit cell]]. Although a lot of the following treatment is only true for those systems, it is easily generalizable to any crystalline topological insulator. Some notable examples of two-band systems are [[graphene]] and the [[Su–Schrieffer–Heeger model|Su-Shrieffer-Heeger model]] (describing [[polyacetylene]]). By separating the degrees of freedom from inside and outside the cell, one can write the wavefunction as<math display="block">|\psi_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_m e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot \mathbf{R}_m}|m\rangle \otimes |\alpha\rangle
\equiv |\mathbf{k}\rangle \otimes |\alpha\rangle</math>where <math>m</math> labels the unit cell, <math>\mathbf{R}_m</math> are [[Crystal structure|lattice vectors]], <math>N</math> is the number of unit cells (which may or may not be infinite) and <math>|\alpha\rangle</math> is the internal state of a unit cell, which in our case can be generically written <math>|\alpha\rangle = a|A\rangle + b|B\rangle</math> (where A and B are the internal degrees of freedom).<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Asbóth |first=J. K. |url=https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.02295 |title=A Short Course on Topological Insulators: Band-structure topology and edge states in one and two dimensions |last2=Oroszlány |first2=L. |last3=Pályi |first3=A. |date=September 9, 2015 |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-25607-8}}</ref> Due to [[Bloch's theorem]], this basis block-diagonalizes the Hamiltonian. One such block, <math>h_\mathbf{k}\equiv \langle \mathbf{k} | H | \mathbf{k} \rangle</math> corresponding to the quasimomentum <math>\mathbf{k}</math>, can be represented by a <math>2 \times 2</math> [[hermitian matrix]] for the two-band case (this matrix is often called the Bloch Hamiltonian). Any <math>2 \times 2</math> hermitian matrix can be written as a linear combination of [[Pauli matrices]], <math>\sigma^1, \sigma^2</math> and <math>\sigma^3</math> and the [[identity matrix]]. Hence any two-band periodic Hamiltonian can be written as<ref name=":02" /><math display="block">h_\mathbf{k}=d_i(\mathbf{k})\sigma^i+d_0(\mathbf{k})I</math>where [[Einstein notation|summation over repeated indices]] is assumed, <math>d_i</math> is a three dimensional real valued vector, and <math>I</math> is the identity matrix. The advantage of this formulation is that the Hamiltonian can now be viewed as a vector in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>, and n-dimensional subsets of the [[Brillouin zone]] now parametrize a n-dimensional surfaces in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>. In this sense, we can think of <math>\mathbf{d}=(d_1,d_2,d_3)</math> as a mapping between two spaces:<math display="block">\mathbf{d} : T^d \to \mathbb{R}^3</math><math>T^d</math> corresponds to k-space and <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> in our case corresponds to the space of <math>2 \times 2</math> hermitian matrices. Moreover, this basis of the Hamiltonian allows to perform [[3D rotation group#Connection between SO(3) and SU(2)|scalar products and rotations of vectors]] <math>\mathbf{d}</math>. The latter is of particular interest since <math>\sigma^3</math> is diagonal, meaning  <math>h_\mathbf{k}</math> can be diagonalized by rotating <math>\mathbf{d}</math> to be parallel to the <math>z</math> axis. Therefore, there exists a unitary matrix of the form <math>R_\mathbf{k}=\exp[i\mathbf{\theta(\mathbf{k}})\cdot \frac{\mathbf{\sigma}}{2}]</math> such that <math display="block">R_\mathbf{k} h_\mathbf{k} R_\mathbf{k}^\dagger=

\begin{pmatrix}
 |\mathbf{d(\mathbf{k})}|+d_0 & 0\\
 0 & -|\mathbf{d(\mathbf{k})}|+d_0 
\end{pmatrix}</math>where <math>\mathbf{\theta}(\mathbf{k})</math> is the axis of rotation, and its magnitude determines the angle of rotation. The energies can be deduced from the fact that <math>(h_\mathbf{k}-d_0I)^2=d_i d^i</math>. Most importantly, the rotation <math>R_\mathbf{k}</math> only involves the direction of <math>\mathbf{d}</math>, thus the eigenstates of <math>h_\mathbf{k}</math> do not depend on its magnitude, and so does any quantity that only involves eigenstates.

==== Connection to topology ====
An important examples of such a quantity is the [[Berry connection and curvature|Berry connection]]: <math display="block">\mathcal{A}_{\alpha,\beta}(\mathbf{k})\equiv i \langle \psi_\alpha(\mathbf{k}) |\nabla_\mathbf{k}|\psi_\beta(\mathbf{k})\rangle</math>where <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are band indices. Its integral over a path gives the [[geometric phase]], which corresponds to the phase gained by a state during [[Adiabatic theorem|adiabatic evolution]] that is not due to the change in energy. In the context of band structure, such a geometric phase is called a [[Zak phase]]. In two dimensional materials, an integral of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> over the Brillouin zone gives the [[Quantum Hall effect|Hall conductance]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tong |first=David |url=https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qhe.html |title=The Quantum Hall Effect |date=2016}}</ref> and its integral can also be used to compute the [[Polarization density#Polarization ambiguity|polarization]] of a crystal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Spaldin |first=Nicola A. |date=2012 |title=A beginner's guide to the modern theory of polarization |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022459612003234?via%3Dihub |journal=Journal of Solid State Chemistry |volume=195 |pages=2–10}}</ref> Notice that the Berry connection is not gauge invariant, but its integral over a closed path is, therefore only the integral of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> over a closed domain can correspond to an observable quantity. <math>\mathcal{A}</math> depends only on the direction of <math>\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})</math>, <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{k})</math>, which can be thought of as a mapping from d-torus <math>T^d</math> to the [[Sphere|2-sphere]] <math>S^2</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dalibard |first=Jean |url=https://www.college-de-france.fr/fr/agenda/cours/la-matiere-topologique-et-son-exploration-avec-les-gaz-quantiques |title=La matière topologique et son exploration avec les gaz quantiques |date=2017}}</ref><math display="block">\hat{\mathbf{d}}: T^d \to S^2</math>Let <math>\mathcal{O} \in \mathbb{R}</math> be a physically observable quantity obtained by integrating the Berry phase over <math>T^d</math>, the Brillouin zone (for example the Hall conductance). This can be seen as the composite map <math>\mathcal{O}(\hat{\mathbf{d}}(T^d))</math>
[[File:P1S2all.jpg|thumb|373x373px|Two curves or said to be homotopically equivalent if they can be smoothly deformed into one another. Every loop on the 2-sphere can be smoothly deformed into a single point, hence all looops on the 2-sphere are homotopically equivalent.]]
[[File:Winding_Number_3.svg|thumb|168x168px|An example of a loop with winding number 3. The curves are not superposed so that the loop can be understood better. In the example that's discussed in this section, the curve lives on <math>S^1</math>, thus it's the projection of what is shown here on the unit circle.]]
<math display="block">\mathcal{O}: T^d \to S^2 \to \mathbb{R}</math>Thus such an observable must depend on <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(T^d)</math>. Let's consider <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(T^d)</math> and <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}'(T^d)</math>, two continuous mappings from <math>T^d</math> to <math>S^2</math>. If <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(T^d)</math> can be smoothly deformed into <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}'(T^d)</math>, they are said to be [[Homotopy|homotopically equivalent]].<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |last=Texeira Pires |first=Antonio Sergio |title=A Brief Introduction to Topology and Differential Geometry in Condensed Matter Physics |date=2019 |publisher=Morgan & Caypool Publishers |isbn=978-1-64327-374-7}}</ref> For example a loop on a sphere can be thought as such a mapping where <math>T^d=S^1</math>is the unit circle and all loops on a sphere are homotopically equivalent since they can all be smoothly deformed into a single point. If instead <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}: T^d \to S^1</math>, which is the case when <math>\mathbf{d}</math> lies on a plane (and thus the Bloch Hamiltonian is only composed of two Pauli matrices), this is no longer the case: not all loops on a circle can be contracted to a point. A set of homotopically equivalent mappings is called an [[equivalence class]]. Given a [[manifold]] <math>M</math>, the set of equivalence classes of mappings between <math>M</math> and <math>S^n</math>, with the operation of composition of the mappings, is called the [[Homotopy group|n-th homotopy group]] of <math>M</math>, noted <math>\pi_n(M)</math>.<ref name=":13" /> The relevant homotopy groups for two-band systems are <math>\pi_2(T^d)</math> and <math>\pi_1(T^d)</math> since we can only consider mappings from closed subsets of the Brillouin zone (<math>T^d</math>) to the 2-sphere <math>S^2</math> or the circle <math>S^1</math>(which is a subset of <math>S^2</math>). For example if we take <math>S^1</math>, the unit circle, then <math>\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb{Z}</math>: when we map a circle to a circle, we get a loop that lives on the perimeter of the circle, such loops can wind an integer number of times around the circle and loops with a different [[winding number]] cannot be deformed into one another. Another example is <math>\pi_2(S^1)=\{I\}</math> since every loop on a sphere can be smoothly deformed into a single point, hence all mappings from the circle to the 2-sphere are homotopically equivalent. A number that labels an element of the homotopy group is called a [[Topological property|topological invariant]]. An example of such a topological invariant for the first homotopy group of a circle is the [[winding number]] mentioned before.<ref name=":13" /> In this case <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{k})=\cos(\phi(\mathbf{k}))\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\sin(\phi(\mathbf{k}))\hat{\mathbf{y}}</math> and one way to compute the [[winding number]] <math>\nu</math> is <math display="block">\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma d\phi(\mathbf{k})</math>

==== Insulating phases as elements of the homotopy group ====
The [[unit vector]] <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{k})</math> can be defined as <math>\frac{\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})}{|\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})|}</math> as long as <math>|\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})| \neq 0</math>, therefore, curves or surfaces passing through the origin cannot be continuously mapped to the 2-sphere. Two elements of the [[homotopy group]] are separated by a discontinuity and hence they must describe curves or surfaces <math>\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})</math> that can only be deformed into one another by passing through the origin in <math>(d_1,d_2,d_3)</math>space. Looking at the form of two-band Bloch Hamiltonian given above, one can see that if <math>|\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})| = 0</math>, the Hamiltonian becomes [[Degenerate energy levels|degenerate]], and thus two [[Electronic band structure|bands]] must be touching. Therefore, according to [[Electronic band structure|band theory]], a two-band Hamiltonian describes a [[Electrical conductor|conductor]] if <math>\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})</math> passes through the origin at some point in the Brillouin zone. One can deduce from this that two elements of the homotopy group correspond to two insulating Hamiltonians separated by a conducting phase, or alternatively, those two Hamiltonians are not [[Adiabatic theorem|adiabatically connected]].<ref name=":02" /> Pairs of Hamiltonians representing different elements of the homotopy group are said to have a different topology.

Integrals of the [[Berry connection and curvature|Berry connection]] <math>\mathcal{A}</math> over the Brillouin zone cannot vary smoothly between Hamiltonians of different topology since they depend on <math>\hat{\mathbf{d}}(\mathcal{BZ})</math> which cannot vary smoothly between those two Hamiltonians. It turns out that this integral is a [[Topological property|topological invariant]]. For example, in the case where <math>\mathbf{d}</math> lies on a plane, it can be shown, using the unitary matrix that diagonalises the Hamiltonian, <math>R_\mathbf{k}=\exp[i\mathbf{\theta(\mathbf{k}})\cdot \frac{\mathbf{\sigma}}{2}]</math>, that <math>\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{k})=\mathbf{\nabla}_\mathbf{k}\phi(\mathbf{k})</math> (where <math>\phi</math> is the angle on the circle), hence<math display="block">\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\mathcal{BZ} d\mathbf{\Sigma}\cdot \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{k})</math>is a winding number.<ref name=":02" /> As has been mentioned before, the topological invariants are gauge invariant and thus can be physically observable quantities. The most famous of such quantities are the number of [[edge states]] (see for example the [[Su–Schrieffer–Heeger model|Su-Schrieffer-Heeger]] model) and the Hall conductance in the [[Quantum Hall effect#Integer quantum Hall effect|integer quantum Hall effect]].

== Experimental realization ==
2D Topological insulators were first realized in system containing [[HgTe]] quantum wells sandwiched between [[cadmium telluride]] in 2007.

The first 3D topological insulator to be realized experimentally was [[Bismuth antimonide|Bi<sub>1 − x</sub> Sb <sub>x</sub>]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Fu |first1=Liang |last2=Kane |first2=C. It was proposed in 2008 and 2009 that topological insulators are best understood not as surface conductors per se, but as bulk 3D magnetoelectrics with a quantized [[magnetoelectric]] effect.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Qi |first1=Xiao-Liang |last2=Hughes |first2=Taylor L. |last3=Zhang |first3=Shou-Cheng |date=2008-11-24 |title=Topological field theory of time-reversal invariant insulators |journal=Physical Review B |publisher=American Physical Society (APS) |volume=78 |issue=19 |article-number=195424 |arxiv=0802.3537 |bibcode=2008PhRvB..78s5424Q |doi=10.1103/physrevb.78.195424 |issn=1098-0121 |s2cid=117659977}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Essin |first1=Andrew M. |last2=Moore |first2=Joel E. |last3=Vanderbilt |first3=David |date=2009-04-10 |title=Magnetoelectric Polarizability and Axion Electrodynamics in Crystalline Insulators |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=102 |issue=14 |article-number=146805 |arxiv=0810.2998 |bibcode=2009PhRvL.102n6805E |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.102.146805 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=19392469 |s2cid=1133717}}</ref>   This can be revealed by placing topological insulators in magnetic field. The effect can be described in language similar to that of the hypothetical [[Axion|axion particle]] of [[particle physics]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wilczek |first=Frank |date=1987-05-04 |title=Two applications of axion electrodynamics |journal=Physical Review Letters |publisher=American Physical Society (APS) |volume=58 |issue=18 |pages=1799–1802 |bibcode=1987PhRvL..58.1799W |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.58.1799 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=10034541}}</ref>   The effect was reported by researchers at [[Johns Hopkins University]] and [[Rutgers University]] using [[N. Peter Armitage|THz spectroscopy]] who showed that the Faraday rotation was quantized by the fine structure constant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Liang |last2=Salehi |first2=M. |last3=Koirala |first3=N. |last4=Moon |first4=J. |last5=Oh |first5=S. |last6=Armitage |first6=N. P. |year=2016 |title=Quantized Faraday and Kerr rotation and axion electrodynamics of a 3D topological insulator |journal=Science |volume=354 |issue=6316 |pages=1124–7 |arxiv=1603.04317 |bibcode=2016Sci...354.1124W |doi=10.1126/science.aaf5541 |pmid=27934759 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2012, topological [[Kondo effect|Kondo]] insulators were identified in [[samarium hexaboride]], which is a bulk insulator at low temperatures.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Samuel Reich |first=Eugenie |year=2012 |title=Hopes surface for exotic insulator: Findings by three teams may solve a 40-year-old mystery |journal=Nature |publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC |volume=492 |issue=7428 |page=165 |bibcode=2012Natur.492..165S |doi=10.1038/492165a |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=23235853 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dzero |first1=Maxim |last2=Sun |first2=Kai |last3=Galitski |first3=Victor |author-link3=Victor Galitski |last4=Coleman |first4=Piers |author-link4=Piers Coleman |date=2010-03-12 |title=Topological Kondo Insulators |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=104 |issue=10 |article-number=106408 |arxiv=0912.3750 |bibcode=2010PhRvL.104j6408D |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.104.106408 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=20366446 |s2cid=119270507}}</ref>

In 2014, it was shown that magnetic components, like the ones in [[spin-transfer torque|spin-torque computer memory]], can be manipulated by topological insulators.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Weird materials could make faster computers |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/weird-materials-could-make-faster-computers |access-date=2014-07-23 |magazine=Science News}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mellnik |first1=A. R |last2=Lee |first2=J. S |last3=Richardella |first3=A |last4=Grab |first4=J. L |last5=Mintun |first5=P. J |last6=Fischer |first6=M. H |last7=Vaezi |first7=A |last8=Manchon |first8=A |last9=Kim |first9=E. -A |last10=Samarth |first10=N |last11=Ralph |first11=D. C |year=2014 |title=Spin-transfer torque generated by a topological insulator |journal=Nature |volume=511 |issue=7510 |pages=449–451 |arxiv=1402.1124 |bibcode=2014Natur.511..449M |doi=10.1038/nature13534 |pmid=25056062 |s2cid=205239604}}</ref> The effect is related to [[metal–insulator transition]]s ([[Bose–Hubbard model]]).{{Citation needed|date=January 2018}}

=== Floquet topological insulators ===
Topological insulators are challenging to synthesize, and limited in topological phases accessible with solid-state materials.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ando |first=Yoichi |date=2013-10-15 |title=Topological Insulator Materials |journal=Journal of the Physical Society of Japan |volume=82 |issue=10 |article-number=102001 |arxiv=1304.5693 |bibcode=2013JPSJ...82j2001A |doi=10.7566/jpsj.82.102001 |issn=0031-9015 |s2cid=55912821}}</ref> This has motivated the search for topological phases on the systems that simulate the same principles underlying topological insulators. Discrete time quantum walks (DTQW) have been proposed for making Floquet topological insulators (FTI). This&nbsp; periodically driven system simulates an effective ([[Floquet theory|Floquet]]) Hamiltonian that is topologically nontrivial.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cayssol |first1=Jérôme |last2=Dóra |first2=Balázs |last3=Simon |first3=Ferenc |last4=Moessner |first4=Roderich |date=2013-01-28 |title=Floquet topological insulators |journal=Physica Status Solidi RRL |volume=7 |issue=1–2 |pages=101–108 |arxiv=1211.5623 |bibcode=2013PSSRR...7..101C |doi=10.1002/pssr.201206451 |issn=1862-6254 |s2cid=52082807}}</ref> This system replicates the effective Hamiltonians from all universal classes of 1- to 3-D topological insulators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kitaev |first1=Alexei |last2=Lebedev |first2=Vladimir |last3=Feigel'man |first3=Mikhail |date=2009 |title=Periodic table for topological insulators and superconductors |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |publisher=AIP |volume=1134 |issue=1 |pages=22–30 |arxiv=0901.2686 |bibcode=2009AIPC.1134...22K |doi=10.1063/1.3149495 |s2cid=14320124}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Panahiyan |first1=S. |last2=Fritzsche |first2=S. |date=2021-01-05 |title=Toward simulation of topological phenomena with one-, two-, and three-dimensional quantum walks |journal=Physical Review A |volume=103 |issue=1 |article-number=012201 |arxiv=2005.08720 |bibcode=2021PhRvA.103a2201P |doi=10.1103/physreva.103.012201 |issn=2469-9926 |s2cid=218674364}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kitagawa |first1=Takuya |last2=Rudner |first2=Mark S. |last3=Berg |first3=Erez |last4=Demler |first4=Eugene |date=2010-09-24 |title=Exploring topological phases with quantum walks |journal=Physical Review A |volume=82 |issue=3 |article-number=033429 |arxiv=1003.1729 |bibcode=2010PhRvA..82c3429K |doi=10.1103/physreva.82.033429 |issn=1050-2947 |s2cid=21800060}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=Khazali |first=Mohammadsadegh |date=2022-03-03 |title=Discrete-Time Quantum-Walk & Floquet Topological Insulators via Distance-Selective Rydberg-Interaction |url=https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2022-03-03-664/ |journal=Quantum |language=en-GB |volume=6 |page=664 |arxiv=2101.11412 |bibcode=2022Quant...6..664K |doi=10.22331/q-2022-03-03-664 |s2cid=246635019 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Interestingly, topological properties of Floquet topological insulators could be controlled via an external periodic drive&nbsp; rather than an external magnetic field. An atomic lattice empowered by distance selective Rydberg interaction could simulate different classes of FTI over a couple of hundred sites and steps in 1, 2 or 3 dimensions.<ref name=":9" /> The long-range interaction allows designing topologically ordered periodic boundary conditions, further enriching the realizable topological phases.<ref name=":9" />

=== Synthesis ===
Topological insulators can be grown using different methods such as [[Metal organic chemical vapor deposition|metal-organic chemical vapor deposition]] (MOCVD),<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Alegria|first1=L. D.|last2=Schroer|first2=M. D.|last3=Chatterjee|first3=A.|last4=Poirier|first4=G. R.|last5=Pretko|first5=M.|last6=Patel|first6=S. K.|last7=Petta|first7=J. R.|date=2012-08-06|title=Structural and Electrical Characterization of {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} Nanostructures Grown by Metal–Organic Chemical Vapor Deposition|journal=Nano Letters|language=EN|volume=12|issue=9|pages=4711–4|doi=10.1021/nl302108r|pmid=22827514|issn=1530-6984|arxiv=1108.4978|bibcode=2012NanoL..12.4711A|s2cid=28030427}}</ref>
[[physical vapor deposition]] (PVD),<ref>{{Cite journal|date= 2017  |title=Large-Area and Transferred High-Quality Three-Dimensional Topological Insulator Bi2–x Sb x Te3–y Se y Ultrathin Film by Catalyst-Free Physical Vapor Deposition|journal= Nano Letters|language=en|volume=17|issue=4|pages=2354–60|doi= 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b05260|last1=Tu, Ngoc Han|first1=Tanabe, Yoichi|last2=Satake, Yosuke|first2=Huynh, Khuong Kim|last3=Le, Phuoc Huu|first3=Matsushita, Stephane Yu|last4=Tanigaki, Katsumi|pmid=28337910|arxiv=1601.06541|bibcode=2017NanoL..17.2354T|s2cid=206738534}}</ref> solvothermal synthesis,<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2003-06-01|title=Preparation and characterization of wire-like {{chem|Sb|2|Se|3}} and flake-like {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} nanocrystals|journal=Journal of Crystal Growth|language=en|volume=253|issue=1–4|pages=445–451|doi=10.1016/S0022-0248(03)01019-4|issn=0022-0248|last1=Wang|first1=Debao|last2=Yu|first2=Dabin|last3=Mo|first3=Maosong|last4=Liu|first4=Xianming|last5=Qian|first5=Yitai|bibcode=2003JCrGr.253..445W}}</ref>  sonochemical technique<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2004-11-15|title=Sonochemical synthesis of bismuth selenide nanobelts at room temperature|journal=Journal of Crystal Growth|language=en|volume=271|issue=3–4|pages=456–461|doi=10.1016/j.jcrysgro.2004.08.015|issn=0022-0248|last1=Cui|first1=Hongmei|last2=Liu|first2=Hong|last3=Wang|first3=Jiyang|last4=Li|first4=Xia|last5=Han|first5=Feng|last6=Boughton|first6=R.I.|bibcode=2004JCrGr.271..456C}}</ref>  and [[molecular beam epitaxy]][[File:Molecular Beam Epitaxy.png|thumb|250x250px|Schematic of the components of a MBE system]]
(MBE).<ref name=":3" />  MBE has so far been the most common experimental technique. The growth of thin film topological insulators is governed by weak [[van der Waals interactions]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jerng|first1=Sahng-Kyoon|last2=Joo|first2=Kisu|last3=Kim|first3=Youngwook|last4=Yoon|first4=Sang-Moon|last5=Lee|first5=Jae Hong|last6=Kim|first6=Miyoung|last7=Kim|first7=Jun Sung|last8=Yoon|first8=Euijoon|last9=Chun|first9=Seung-Hyun|date=2013|title=Ordered growth of topological insulator {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} thin films on dielectric amorphous SiO2 by MBE|journal=Nanoscale|language=en|volume=5|issue=21|pages=10618–22|doi=10.1039/C3NR03032F|pmid=24056725|issn=2040-3364|arxiv=1308.3817|bibcode=2013Nanos...510618J|s2cid=36212915}}</ref> The weak interaction allows to exfoliate the thin film from bulk crystal with a clean and perfect surface. The van der Waals interactions in epitaxy also known as van der Waals epitaxy (VDWE), is a phenomenon governed by weak van der Waals interactions between layered materials of different or same elements<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Geim|first1=A. K.|last2=Grigorieva|first2=I. V.|date=2013|title=Van der Waals heterostructures|journal=Nature|language=En|volume=499|issue=7459|pages=419–425|doi=10.1038/nature12385|pmid=23887427|issn=0028-0836|arxiv=1307.6718|s2cid=205234832}}</ref> in which the materials are stacked on top of each other. This approach allows the growth of layered topological insulators on other substrates for [[heterostructure]] and [[integrated circuit]]s.<ref name=":4" />

=== MBE growth of topological insulators ===
Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) is an [[epitaxy]] method for the growth of a crystalline material on a crystalline substrate to form an ordered layer.  MBE is performed in [[Vacuum|high vacuum]] or [[ultra-high vacuum]], the elements are heated in different electron beam evaporators until they [[Sublimation (phase transition)|sublime]]. The gaseous elements then condense on the wafer where they react with each other to form [[single crystal]]s.

MBE is an appropriate technique for the growth of high quality single-crystal films.  In order to avoid a huge [[Lattice constant#Lattice matching|lattice mismatch]] and [[Crystallographic defect|defects]] at the interface, the substrate and thin film are expected to have similar lattice constants.  MBE has an advantage over other methods due to the fact that the synthesis is performed in high vacuum hence resulting in less contamination.  Additionally,  lattice defect is reduced due to the ability to influence the growth rate and the ratio of species of source materials present at the substrate interface.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Heremans|first1=Joseph P.|last2=Cava|first2=Robert J.|last3=Samarth|first3=Nitin|date=2017-09-05|title=Tetradymites as thermoelectrics and topological insulators|journal=Nature Reviews Materials|language=En|volume=2|issue=10|page=17049|doi=10.1038/natrevmats.2017.49|issn=2058-8437|bibcode=2017NatRM...217049H}}</ref> Furthermore,  in MBE,  samples can be grown layer by layer which results in flat surfaces with smooth interface for engineered heterostructures.  Moreover,  MBE synthesis technique benefits from the ease of moving a topological insulator sample from the growth chamber to a characterization chamber such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) or [[scanning tunneling microscopy]] (STM) studies.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Topological+Insulators:+Fundamentals+and+Perspectives-p-9783527337026|title=Topological Insulators: Fundamentals and Perspectives|date=2015-06-29|website=Wiley.com|language=en-us|access-date=2018-07-29}}</ref>

Due to the weak van der Waals bonding, which relaxes the lattice-matching condition, TI can be grown on a wide variety of substrates<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=He|first1=Liang|last2=Kou|first2=Xufeng|last3=Wang|first3=Kang L.|date=2013-01-31|title=Review of 3D topological insulator thin-film growth by molecular beam epitaxy and potential applications|journal=Physica Status Solidi RRL|language=en|volume=7|issue=1–2|pages=50–63|doi=10.1002/pssr.201307003|issn=1862-6254|bibcode=2013PSSRR...7...50H|s2cid=97544002|doi-access=free}}</ref> such as Si(111),<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2011-10-31|title=Epitaxial growth of topological insulator {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} film on Si(111) with atomically sharp interface|journal=Thin Solid Films|language=en|volume=520|issue=1|pages=224–9|doi=10.1016/j.tsf.2011.07.033|issn=0040-6090|last1=Bansal|first1=Namrata|last2=Kim|first2=Yong Seung|last3=Edrey|first3=Eliav|last4=Brahlek|first4=Matthew|last5=Horibe|first5=Yoichi|last6=Iida|first6=Keiko|last7=Tanimura|first7=Makoto|last8=Li|first8=Guo-Hong|last9=Feng|first9=Tian|last10=Lee|first10=Hang-Dong|last11=Gustafsson|first11=Torgny|last12=Andrei|first12=Eva|last13=Oh|first13=Seongshik|arxiv=1104.3438|bibcode=2011TSF...520..224B|s2cid=118512981}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Guanhua|last2=Qin|first2=Huajun|last3=Teng|first3=Jing|last4=Guo|first4=Jiandong|last5=Guo|first5=Qinlin|last6=Dai|first6=Xi|last7=Fang|first7=Zhong|last8=Wu|first8=Kehui|date=2009-08-03|title=Quintuple-layer epitaxy of thin films of topological insulator {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}}|journal=Applied Physics Letters|language=en|volume=95|issue=5|page=053114|doi=10.1063/1.3200237|issn=0003-6951|arxiv=0906.5306|bibcode=2009ApPhL..95e3114Z}}</ref>  {{chem|link=Aluminium oxide|Al|2|O|3}}, [[GaAs]](111),<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Richardella|first1=A.|last2=Zhang|first2=D. M.|last3=Lee|first3=J. S.|last4=Koser|first4=A.|last5=Rench|first5=D. W.|last6=Yeats|first6=A. L.|last7=Buckley|first7=B. B.|last8=Awschalom|first8=D. D.|last9=Samarth|first9=N.|date=2010-12-27|title=Coherent heteroepitaxy of {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} on GaAs (111)B|journal=Applied Physics Letters|language=en|volume=97|issue=26|page=262104|doi=10.1063/1.3532845|arxiv=1012.1918|bibcode=2010ApPhL..97z2104R|issn=0003-6951|doi-access=free}}</ref>
[[InP]](111), [[CdS]](0001) and {{chem|link=Yttrium iron garnet|Y|3|Fe|5|O|12}} .

=== PVD growth of topological insulators ===
The physical vapor deposition (PVD) technique does not suffer from the disadvantages of the exfoliation method and, at the same time, it is much simpler and cheaper than the fully controlled growth by molecular-beam epitaxy. The PVD method enables a reproducible synthesis of single crystals of various layered quasi-two-dimensional materials including topological insulators (i.e., {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}}, {{chem|Bi|2|Te|3}}).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kong|first1=D.|last2=Dang|first2=W.|last3=Cha|first3=J.J.|last4=Li|first4=H.|last5=Meister|first5=S.|last6=Peng|first6=H. K.|last7=Cui|first7=Y|date=2010|title=SFew-layer nanoplates of {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} and {{chem|Bi|2|Te|3}} with highly tunable chemical potential|journal=Nano Letters|language=EN|volume=10|issue=6|pages=2245–50|doi = 10.1021/nl101260j|pmid=20486680|arxiv=1004.1767|bibcode=2010NanoL..10.2245K|s2cid=37687875}}</ref> The resulted single crystals have a well-defined crystallographic orientation; their composition, thickness, size, and the surface density on the desired substrate can be controlled.
The thickness control is particularly important for 3D TIs in which the trivial (bulky) electronic channels usually dominate the transport properties and mask the response of the topological (surface) modes. By reducing the thickness, one lowers the contribution of trivial bulk channels into the total conduction, thus forcing the topological modes to carry the electric current.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stolyarov|first1=V.S.|last2=Yakovlev|first2=D.S.|last3=Kozlov|first3=S.N.|last4=Skryabina|first4=O.V.|last5=Lvov|first5=D.S.|date=2020|title=Josephson current mediated by ballistic topological states in Bi2Te2.3Se0.7 single nanocrystals|journal=Communications Materials |language=EN|volume=1|issue=1 |page=38| doi = 10.1038/s43246-020-0037-y|bibcode=2020CoMat...1...38S|s2cid=220295733|doi-access=free}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]]  Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/  Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref>

==== Bismuth-based topological insulators ====
Thus far, the field of topological insulators has been focused on bismuth and antimony [[chalcogenide]] based materials such as {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}}, {{chem|Bi|2|Te|3}}, {{chem|Sb|2|Te|3}} or [[Bismuth antimonide|Bi<sub>1 − x</sub>Sb<sub>x</sub>]], Bi<sub>1.1</sub>Sb<sub>0.9</sub>Te<sub>2</sub>S.<ref name="NatureComm"/>  The choice of chalcogenides is related to the van der Waals relaxation of the lattice matching strength which restricts the number of materials and substrates.<ref name=":5" />  Bismuth chalcogenides have been studied extensively for TIs and their applications in [[thermoelectric materials]].  The van der Waals interaction in TIs exhibit important features due to low surface energy.  For instance, the surface of {{chem|link=Bismuth telluride|Bi|2|Te|3}} is usually terminated by Te due to its low surface energy.<ref name=":3" />

Bismuth chalcogenides have been successfully grown on different substrates. In particular, Si has been a good substrate for the successful growth of  {{chem|Bi|2|Te|3}} . However, the use of sapphire as substrate has not been so encouraging due to a large mismatch of about 15%.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Ginley|first1=Theresa P.|last2=Wang|first2=Yong|last3=Law|first3=Stephanie|author3-link=Stephanie Law (materials scientist)|date=2016-11-23|title=Topological Insulator Film Growth by Molecular Beam Epitaxy: A Review|journal=Crystals|language=en|volume=6|issue=11|page=154|doi=10.3390/cryst6110154|doi-access=free|bibcode=2016Cryst...6..154G }}</ref> The selection of appropriate substrate can improve the overall properties of TI. The use of buffer layer can reduce the lattice match hence improving the electrical properties of TI.<ref name=":6" /> {{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}} can be grown on top of various Bi<sub>2 − x</sub>In<sub>x</sub>Se<sub>3</sub> buffers.  Table 1 shows {{chem|link=Bismuth selenide|Bi|2|Se|3}}, {{chem|Bi|2|Te|3}}, {{chem|link=Antimony telluride|Sb|2|Te|3}}  on different substrates and the resulting lattice mismatch. Generally,  regardless of the substrate used, the resulting films have a textured surface that is characterized by pyramidal single-crystal domains with quintuple-layer steps. The size and relative proportion of these pyramidal domains vary with factors that include film thickness, lattice mismatch with the substrate and interfacial chemistry-dependent film nucleation. The synthesis of thin films have the stoichiometry problem due to the high vapor pressures of the elements. Thus, binary tetradymites are extrinsically doped as n-type ({{chem|Bi|2|Se|3}}, {{chem|Bi|2|Te|3}} ) or p-type ({{chem|Sb|2|Te|3}} ).<ref name=":5" /> Due to the weak van der Waals bonding, graphene is one of the preferred substrates for TI growth despite the large lattice mismatch.

=== Identification ===
The first step of topological insulators identification takes place right after synthesis, meaning without breaking the vacuum and moving the sample to an atmosphere. That could be done by using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) or scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) techniques.<ref name=":7" /> Further measurements includes structural and chemical probes such as X-ray diffraction and energy-dispersive spectroscopy but depending on the sample quality, the lack of sensitivity could remain. Transport measurements cannot uniquely pinpoint the <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topology by definition of the state.

== Classification ==
{{Main|Periodic table of topological insulators and topological superconductors}}
[[Bloch's theorem]] allows a full characterization of the wave propagation properties of a material by assigning a matrix to each wave vector in the [[Brillouin zone]].

Mathematically, this assignment creates a [[vector bundle]]. Different materials will have different wave propagation properties, and thus different vector bundles. If we consider all insulators (materials with a band gap), this creates a space of vector bundles. It is the topology of this space (modulo trivial bands) from which the "topology" in topological insulators arises.<ref name=":12" />

Specifically, the number of [[Connected component (topology)|connected components]] of the space indicates how many different "islands" of insulators exist amongst the metallic states. Insulators in the connected component containing the vacuum state are identified as "trivial", and all other insulators as "topological". The connected component in which an insulator lies can be identified with a number, referred to as a "topological invariant".<ref name=":12" />

This space can be restricted under the presence of symmetries, changing the resulting topology. Although [[Unitary matrix|unitary]] symmetries are usually significant in quantum mechanics, they have no effect on the topology here.<ref>{{Cite web |title=10 symmetry classes and the periodic table of topological insulators |url=https://topocondmat.org/w8_general/classification.html |access-date=2022-10-11 |website=topocondmat.org}}</ref> Instead, the three symmetries typically considered are time-reversal symmetry, particle-hole symmetry, and chiral symmetry (also called sublattice symmetry). Mathematically, these are represented as, respectively: an [[Antiunitary operator|anti-unitary operator]] which commutes with the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]]; an anti-unitary operator which [[Anticommutative property|anti-commutes]] with the Hamiltonian; and a unitary operator which anti-commutes with the Hamiltonian. All combinations of the three together with each spatial dimension result in the so-called [[Periodic table of topological invariants|periodic table of topological insulators]].<ref name=":12" />

== Future developments ==
The field of topological insulators still needs to be developed. The best bismuth chalcogenide topological insulators have about 10 meV bandgap variation due to the charge. Further development should focus on the examination of both: the presence of high-symmetry electronic bands and simply synthesized materials. One of the candidates is [[Heusler compound|half-Heusler compounds]].<ref name=":7" /> These crystal structures can consist of a large number of elements. Band structures and energy gaps are very sensitive to the valence configuration; because of the increased likelihood of intersite exchange and disorder, they are also very sensitive to specific crystalline configurations. A nontrivial band structure that exhibits band ordering analogous to that of the known 2D and 3D TI materials was predicted in a variety of 18-electron half-Heusler compounds using first-principles calculations.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2013-04-01|title=Prediction of topological insulating behavior in inverse Heusler compounds from first principles|journal=Computational Materials Science|language=en|volume=70|pages=145–149|doi=10.1016/j.commatsci.2012.12.013|issn=0927-0256|last1=Zhang|first1=X.M.|last2=Liu|first2=E.K.|last3=Liu|first3=Z.Y.|last4=Liu|first4=G.D.|last5=Wu|first5=G.H.|last6=Wang|first6=W.H.|arxiv=1210.5816|s2cid=53506226}}</ref> These materials have not yet shown any sign of intrinsic topological insulator behavior in actual experiments.
